---
description: Write the design docs of a project from its PRD, before the code
model: opus
---

# Goal

- Given a PRD (Product Requirement Document), write `docs/02-design.architecture.md` and
  `docs/02.<N>-design.<component>.md` per component
- Design before the code exists: do not write code

## Input

- `<PRD>`: the PRD file, e.g., `docs/01-prd.md`
- `<DOCS_DIR>`: the `docs/` dir of the project, optional
  - If missing, use the dir of `<PRD>`

# Workflow

## Read the Inputs

- Read `<PRD>` and the existing docs in `<DOCS_DIR>`
- Read the existing code and docs that the design must fit
- Read `.claude/skills/architecture.rules.md` and `.claude/skills/C4.rules.md`

## Ask If the PRD Is Unclear

- If a requirement is ambiguous or two requirements conflict:
  - Do not guess
  - Ask the user and wait for the answers

## Split Into Components

- Propose components, each with one responsibility
- Respect the layering rules in `.claude/skills/architecture.rules.md`
- Show the proposal and wait for user confirmation before writing the docs

## Write the Overview

- Create `<DOCS_DIR>/02-design.architecture.md`
- Follow the template `.claude/templates/project_design.template.md`
- Show the context and containers with a PlantUML C4 diagram, per
  `.claude/skills/C4.rules.md`
- Map each requirement `R<N>` of the PRD to its component
  - Link each `R<N>` to its H3 in the PRD, per `.claude/skills/project.rules.md`
    section "Link Requirements and Decisions"

## Write One Doc per Component

- Create `<DOCS_DIR>/02.<N>-design.<component>.md` for each component
- Follow `.claude/skills/project.rules.md` section "Write a Design Doc" and the
  template `.claude/templates/project_design.template.md`
- Record each non-obvious choice in `<DOCS_DIR>/03-decisions.md`, following the
  template `.claude/templates/project_decisions.template.md`
  - Create the file if it does not exist
- Link each decision from the design docs that follow it, per
  `.claude/skills/project.rules.md` section "Link Requirements and Decisions"

## Update the Index

- Add a row for each new doc to `<DOCS_DIR>/README.md`, if the file exists

# Conventions

- Follow `.claude/skills/project.rules.md` for the docs of a project
- Follow `.claude/skills/architecture.rules.md` for layering and interfaces
- Follow `.claude/skills/markdown.rules.md` and `.claude/skills/text.rules.md`
- Say in each file that you create how it was generated, with this line right
  after the title:
  ```markdown
  - Generated by `.claude/skills/architecture.write_design/SKILL.md`
  ```

# Constraints

- Do not implement any code
  - Short snippets (a class interface, a schema, a function signature) are fine
- Do not use this skill to document an existing Python file: use
  `.claude/skills/readme_file.write_architecture/SKILL.md`
- Do not commit any change

# Verification

- [ ] Every requirement of the PRD maps to a component
- [ ] Every component has one responsibility and one design doc
- [ ] The overview has a PlantUML C4 diagram
- [ ] No design doc has a Mermaid C4 diagram
- [ ] Every non-obvious choice is in `03-decisions.md`
- [ ] Every requirement id and decision id in a design doc is a link to its H3
- [ ] No design doc contains full implementation code
- [ ] Each file that you create says that it was generated by
      `.claude/skills/architecture.write_design/SKILL.md`

skills.desc: Copy project emails from Gmail into Asana tasks for Noesis, Tyrn, Tymes
skills.body:
---
description: Copy project emails from Gmail into Asana tasks for Noesis, Tyrn, Tymes
model: sonnet
---

# Goal

- Read the emails in the Gmail mailbox `saggese@gmail.com` about the projects
  `Noesis`, `Tyrn`, and `Tymes`
- Update the Asana board of each project:
  - Copy each email into the comments of the matching task
  - Create new tasks to track the activities that the emails describe
- Write a short plan with links to the Asana tasks and get the user approval before
  any change to Asana

# Conventions

- Follow the rules in `.claude/skills/asana.rules.md`
- Follow the template `.claude/templates/asana_plan.template.md`
- Follow the markdown conventions in `.claude/skills/markdown.rules.md`

# Arguments

- `<PROJECTS>`: projects to process, any of `Noesis`, `Tyrn`, `Tymes`
  - Default: all three
- `<SINCE>`: first day of the email window, in the format `YYYY-MM-DD`
  - Default: 7 days before today

# Workflow

## Resolve the Projects

- Fetch the contributors file:
  ```bash
  > gh api repos/gpsaggese/gpsaggese.github.io/contents/research/contributors.md \
      --jq .content | base64 -d
  ```
  - If `gh` fails, use `WebFetch` on the GitHub URL of the file
- For each project in `<PROJECTS>`, find its section in the file
  - Match the section by the start of its title, as described in
    `.claude/skills/asana.rules.md` `# Source of Truth`
  - Extract `<PROJECT_GID>` from the URL segment `/project/<PROJECT_GID>/` of the
    `Asana board` link
  - Collect the project signals from the other links of the section
  - Collect the names and emails of the people of the project
    - Use the contributors table (`Project` column) when the project has rows
    - Otherwise use the Asana project members from `get_project`
- If a project has no `Asana board` link, report it and skip the project
- Call `get_project` with `<PROJECT_GID>` for each project, before any read or write
  of its tasks
  - Record the name, the permalink, and the members
  - If the call fails, report the error and skip the project
  - Do not use the `workspaces` list of `get_me` as a check, since the workspace can
    be missing from it

## Verify the Mailbox

- Load the Gmail tools with `ToolSearch` if their schemas are not available
- Verify the connected mailbox is `saggese@gmail.com` as described in
  `.claude/skills/asana.rules.md` `# Gmail`
  - Open one recent thread with `get_thread`
  - Check that `saggese@gmail.com` appears in its headers
- If the check fails, stop and tell the user

## Collect the Emails

- For each project, build one Gmail query:
  - `after:<SINCE>`
  - AND an OR group of the contributor emails (`from:`, `to:`, `cc:`), the project
    name, and the project signals
- Run `search_threads` with the query, then `get_thread` for each thread
- For each message, record:
  - Message ID, thread ID, date
  - From, To, Cc
  - Subject, body, attachment names
- Drop the messages that are not relevant, following
  `.claude/skills/asana.rules.md` `## Relevance`
- If one message matches several projects, mark it `Decide`

## Read the Asana State

- For each project, list the tasks with `get_tasks` using `project=<PROJECT_GID>`
  - Request the fields `name,notes,assignee.name,due_on,completed,permalink_url`
  - Include recently completed tasks with `completed_since`
  - Follow the pagination token until all tasks are read
- For the tasks that match some email, read the comments with `get_task_stories`
  using `task_ids` and `resource_subtype=comment_added`
  - Find the markers `[gmail:<MESSAGE_ID>]`
  - Mark the messages that already have a marker as `Skip`

## Match Emails to Tasks

- Give each remaining message one outcome (`Comment`, `New task`, `Skip`, `Decide`)
  following `.claude/skills/asana.rules.md` `# Matching Emails to Tasks`
- Before a `New task` outcome, search the project for duplicates
  - Call `search_tasks` with `projects_any=<PROJECT_GID>` and `text`
  - If a similar task exists, change the outcome to `Comment` on that task
- Note any change to an existing task that an email states explicitly
  - Do not apply it: it goes to `Suggested Field Changes` in the plan

## Write the Plan

- Create `plan-asana.update_from_gmail.md` in the current directory
  - Create it before any change to Asana
- Follow the template `.claude/templates/asana_plan.template.md`
  - Add one H1 section per project
  - Link each task to update with its Asana URL
  - Put each `Decide` message under `Needs Decision`
  - Put each suggested change under `Suggested Field Changes`
- Print the path of the plan and these counts for each project:
  - Comments to add
  - Tasks to create
  - Suggested field changes
  - Skipped messages
  - Messages that need a decision

## Get Approval

- Make no Asana write call before this step is done
- Ask the user to choose one of:
  - Approve the plan as written
  - Approve after the user edits the plan file
  - Cancel
- For each message under `Needs Decision`, ask the user to pick a task or to skip it
- If the user cancels, stop and leave the plan file in place

## Apply the Plan

- Re-read the plan file after approval and execute only the items that it still
  contains
  - Skip an item that the user deleted or left out
- Create the new tasks first with `create_tasks`
  - Set `project_id`, name, notes, section, and due date from the plan
  - Set the assignee only if the plan lists one
- Add the email comments with `add_comment`, oldest message first
  - Use the comment format in `.claude/skills/asana.rules.md` `## Comment Format`
  - Use the plain `text` field and keep the body verbatim
  - If Asana rejects a comment for size, split it into consecutive comments
    - Label the parts as described in `.claude/skills/asana.rules.md`
      `## Comment Format`
- Apply a suggested field change only if the user approved it explicitly
- After each write, update the plan file
  - Tick the item
  - Replace a new task name with a link to the created task
  - Set `Status` to `applied`, or to `partially applied` on any failure
- On an error, stop, record it in the plan, and report it
  - Do not retry in a loop

## Report

- For each project, print:
  - The links to the tasks that received comments
  - The links to the new tasks
  - The messages that were skipped or not applied, with the reason
- State plainly what was not done

# Constraints

- Make no change to Asana before the user approves the plan
- Use Gmail in read-only mode
- Never hard-code Asana project IDs: read them from `research/contributors.md`
- Do not change the name, assignee, due date, or status of an existing task unless
  the user approves the change explicitly
- Do not commit `plan-asana.update_from_gmail.md`
- Do not copy an email that has no link to a project

# Examples

- **Bad** (comment is a summary and has no marker)
  ```text
  Simran says the draft is late
  ```
- **Good** (verbatim body with marker and headers)
  ```text
  [gmail:18f3a1c2d4e5b678] Email copied from Gmail
  From: <NAME> <<EMAIL>>
  To: saggese@gmail.com
  Date: Tue, 10 Nov 2026 09:14:00 -0500
  Subject: Noesis task unit draft
  Link: https://mail.google.com/mail/u/saggese@gmail.com/#all/18f3a1c2d4e5b678

  Hi, I will send the draft of the task unit definition by Friday.
  ```
- **Bad** (new task duplicates an existing one)
  - Plan: create "Write task unit definition" while the task "Task unit draft" exists
- **Good** (comment on the existing task)
  - Plan: add the email as a comment on "Task unit draft"

# Verification

- [ ] The plan file exists and has the line
  `Generated by .claude/skills/asana.update_from_gmail/SKILL.md`
- [ ] Every task to update in the plan has an Asana link
- [ ] No Asana write call happened before the user approved the plan
- [ ] Every copied email starts with the marker `[gmail:<MESSAGE_ID>]`
- [ ] A second run adds no duplicate comments
- [ ] No existing task changed name, assignee, due date, or status without approval
- [ ] The final report lists every skipped or failed item

skills.name: auto_task.create_plan_for_feature
skills.desc: Break a complex feature into an ordered PR plan, with a spec per complex PR
skills.body:
---
description: Break a complex feature into an ordered PR plan, with a spec per complex PR
model: opus
---

# Goal

- Given a request to implement a complex feature, break it into an ordered sequence
  of small, reviewable PRs
- Write a full spec for each PR complex enough to need one
- Do not implement any code

## Input

- The feature/component description, and optionally an existing plan file to extend

# When to Use This Skill

- Use it when one request needs several independently reviewable changes, and at
  least one has a design decision worth writing down
- If the request fits in one PR, skip to "Write a Spec for a PR" with that PR as the
  whole request

# Workflow

## Understand the Request

- Read the related code and the existing code in the target directory
- If the user references a roadmap file (e.g., `plan.<TOPIC>.md` or
  `docs/04-plan.md` per `.claude/skills/project.rules.md`), read it for the exact PR
  scope
  - Use the plan ids (e.g., `PR_M10`) for the `PR<NUM>` bullets and spec files, per
    `.claude/skills/project.rules.md` section "Name the PRs"
- Read the architecture doc of the target directory, if one exists
- If the problem or solution is unclear, follow `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md`
  section "Ask for Clarification Before Executing an Unclear Plan" before
  decomposing

## Decompose into PRs

- Break the feature into an ordered sequence of small, cohesive PRs, each reviewable
  and testable alone
- Prefer PRs that change whole files over splitting one file's logic across PRs
- State each PR's dependencies explicitly
- Merge low-risk, low-complexity PRs instead of over-fragmenting

## Decide Which PRs Need a Full Spec

- A PR needs a full spec if it adds a new interface (class, function, CLI flag),
  makes a non-obvious design decision, or carries meaningful risk (shared/core code,
  hard to reverse, many call sites)
- Small, mechanical, low-risk PRs (rename, config tweak, adding a test) need no
  spec: the plan bullet is enough
- For each PR that needs a spec, write it with "Write a Spec for a PR" below, using
  `<TOPIC>_PR<NUM>` as the topic and the plan file below
  - This produces `spec.<TOPIC>_PR<NUM>.md`

## Write a Spec for a PR

- Create a markdown document following `.claude/templates/specs.template.md`
- Follow `.claude/skills/markdown.rules.md` and `.claude/skills/text.rules.md`
- Save it as `spec.<TOPIC>.md` in the current directory
  - E.g., to spec `PR_P2b` from `plan.md`, save `spec.PR_P2b.md`
  - In a project `docs/` dir, add the slot number: save `06-spec.PR_P2b.md` and read
    `04-plan.md`, per `.claude/skills/project.rules.md` section "Name the Docs with

# Goal

- Create the GH issue, branch, and PR for `<FILE>` before the loop: each `auto_task`
  maps to one GH issue and one branch/PR (see `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md`)

  coding/testing conventions

- Create the GH issue, branch, and (draft) PR for `<FILE>` up front: this is this
  skill's job, not the user's
- Do not commit any code change for a task: committing is the user's decision
- Do not merge any PR: merging is the user's decision

# Workflow

## Confirm the Task List

- Read `<FILE>` and follow `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md` section "Confirm the
  Task List Before Executing" for the format and the problem/solution check

  of Work": one GH issue covers the whole task list in `<FILE>`

  shot with `git_create_issue_and_branch.py`. Unlike `invoke gh_issue_create` and
  `invoke git_branch_create`, it also branches submodules (e.g., `helpers_root`)

  ```bash
  > git_create_issue_and_branch.py \
      --gh_issue_title "<TITLE>" --gh_issue_body "<Description of the task list>" \
      --no_create_pr
  ```

  - Pass `--gh_issue_id <NUM>` instead of `--gh_issue_title` to reuse an issue
  - `--no_create_pr`: a PR needs a commit ahead of `master`. Open it after the first
    task's commit (see "Wait for User to Confirm")
- `git add` (do not commit) `<FILE>` on the new branch, so its plan is tracked from
  the start, per `@.claude/task_instructions.md`

- Keep `<FILE>` updated per `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md` section "Track Task

  - `.claude/skills/github.get_pr_to_pass_local_tests/SKILL.md`

  since there is now a commit to diff against `master`
  - If the task spans several repos (see `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md`
    "Multi-Repo Issues, Branches, and PRs"), open a draft PR in each affected repo,
    then refresh the issue's companion PR links:

    ```bash
    > git_create_issue_and_branch.py --gh_issue_id <NUM> --submodules \
        --update_pr_links
    ```

- After the user confirms the N-th task, do the N+1 task the same way

- [ ] Tests touched by each task pass locally and in CI before the task is marked

- [ ] No commit was made without the user's confirmation

# Goal

- Execute one GitHub issue as a stack of sequential branches and PRs
  - Name each branch `<BASE>_<ID>` (`ID` = 1, 2, 3, ...)
  - Branch each one from the previous branch, so the PRs stack in review order
- Create the whole stack without stopping for review
  - The user reviews, edits, and merges each PR bottom-up later
- Follow `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md` for how tasks are queued, specified,
  and named

## Input

- The user passes a task in the format

# When to Use This Skill

- Use only when tasks favor stacked execution: complete specs, a real dependency
  chain, and a user who prefers one batch review over interruptions
- If a spec is unclear, follow `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md` section "Ask for
  Clarification Before Executing an Unclear Plan". Do not build on a guess
- Resolve all doubts with the user before you start, so the stack runs uninterrupted

# Workflow

## Confirm the Task List

- Follow `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md` section "Confirm the Task List Before
  Executing". Each ordered task is one branch
- Confirm task `<ID+1>` depends only on `<ID>`, not on `master` or earlier tasks
- If the order or a dependency is unclear, ask before starting. A wrong dependency
  means rebasing the whole stack above it

## Create the Issue and the First Branch (`_1`)

- Follow `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md` section "One GitHub Issue Is the Unit
  of Work": one issue covers the whole stack
- Create the issue and the first branch / PR `<BASE>_1`

  ```bash
  > git_create_issue_and_branch.py \
      --gh_issue_title "<TITLE>" --gh_issue_body "<Description of entire stack>" \
      --suffix 1
  ```

- The description of the entire task is
- Commit the file passed by the user (e.g., `tasks.md`)
- Implement task 1, run its tests, commit, push

## Stack Each Following Branch (`_<ID>`)

- For `ID` from 2 to `N`, while still checked out on `<BASE>_<ID-1>`:
  - Derive `<BASE>_<ID>` from the issue, not from the current branch name. Branch
    it from `<BASE>_<ID-1>`, not from `master`:

    ```bash
    > invoke git_branch_create --issue-id <NUM> --suffix <ID> \
        --no-only-branch-from-master --no-create-pr
    ```

    - Do not use `invoke git_branch_next_name`. It appends `_1`, `_2`, ... to the
      current branch, so from `<BASE>_<ID-1>` it gives `<BASE>_<ID-1>_1`
    - Pass `--no-only-branch-from-master`. The default `only_branch_from_master`
      (`True`) branches from `origin/master`, not from the current branch
  - Implement task `<ID>`, run its tests, commit, and push

    ```bash
    > gh pr create --base <BASE>_<ID-1> --head <BASE>_<ID> --title "<TITLE>"
    ```

  - Do not stop for review. Move to `<BASE>_<ID+1>` once `<BASE>_<ID>`'s tests pass

- Confirm each PR's base with `gh pr view <BASE>_<ID> --json baseRefName`

  `ID`

- This is the user's process. It is documented so a later run can resume a stack
- The user reviews, edits, and merges PRs bottom-up, one at a time

    branch was deleted: `gh pr edit <BASE>_<ID> --base master`
  - Sync `<BASE>_<ID>` with the updated `master`, resolve any conflicts, then commit
    and push:

    ```bash
    > invoke git_merge_master
    ```

    - This is a merge, not a rebase. After a squash merge, expect a conflict even on
      identical content: Git cannot tell the squashed commit from the originals

  the user first

  Merge Decisions" and "One GitHub Issue Is the Unit of Work"

  compounds into everything stacked on it
- Do not squash or reorder commits across tasks unless asked
- Keep one task per branch and one PR per task. Do not fold queued tasks together

- [ ] Each PR's base is its parent branch, and `<BASE>_1`'s PR base is `master`

- [ ] Each task's tests passed before its branch was pushed
- [ ] The final report lists every branch and PR in dependency order, with links

skills.body:
---
description: Propagate reviewed changes down an existing PR stack, keeping every PR mergeable
model: sonnet
---

# Goal

- Given the current PR is one branch in a stack of sequential PRs, propagate
  changes reviewed in an earlier PR into every PR stacked on top of it
- Preserve full history: merge forward and commit. Never rebase or force-push
- End with every PR in the stack mergeable, with CI green

# When to Use This Skill

- Use after a PR in the middle or bottom of a stack was reviewed and changed,
  and the branches stacked on top of it need those changes
- Do not use this to build a new stack. Use
  `/auto_task.execute_with_stacked_prs` instead
- Follow `.claude/skills/auto_task.rules.md` section "Ask for Clarification
  Before Executing an Unclear Plan" when a PR's description is unclear. Do not
  guess and merge blind

# Workflow

## Discover the Full Stack

- Get the current PR:
  ```bash
  > gh pr view --json number,title,baseRefName,headRefName,url
  ```
- Walk up from the current PR's `baseRefName`, following each branch's own PR
  (`gh pr list --head <base> --state all`), until reaching the default branch
  (`master`). This is the bottom of the stack
- Walk down from the current PR's `headRefName`, finding the open PR whose
  `baseRefName` equals the previous PR's `headRefName`
  (`gh pr list --base <branch> --state open`). This is the top
- Order the PRs from bottom (based on `master`) to top
- Check whether the bottom PR is behind the default branch:
  ```bash
  > gh pr view <bottom PR> --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus
  ```
  If `mergeable` is `CONFLICTING` (or the branch is just behind), treat the
  default branch as an implicit `PR_0` at the bottom. It needs the same
  merge-forward treatment as every other pair

## Print the Stack

- Print one table with columns `#`, `Branch`, `PR` (`#<NUM> — <title>`), `Base`,
  e.g.:
  ```
  +---+--------------------+-----------------------------------------------+--------+
  | # | Branch             | PR                                             | Base   |
  +---+--------------------+-----------------------------------------------+--------+
  | 1 | ..._invoke_tasks   | #1423 -- auto-pick suffix in git_branch_create | master |
  | 2 | ..._invoke_tasks_2 | #1424 -- unit tests for git_*/gh_* tasks       | #1423  |
  +---+--------------------+-----------------------------------------------+--------+
  ```

## Create and Confirm the Propagation Plan

- Create `plan-auto_task.restack.md` listing, for every consecutive pair
  `(PR_i, PR_i+1)`, including `(master, PR_1)` when the bottom PR is behind the
  default branch:
  - What `PR_i` changed, from its GH description and
    `git diff <base_i>...<head_i>`
  - What must merge into `PR_i+1`, and which files are likely to conflict

skills.body:
---
description: Read, criticize, and propose improvements for a table of content of a book
model: opus
---

# Goal
- Review and criticize the table of content of a book's chapter (or chapters)
- Identify mistakes and improvement opportunities, focusing on factual errors
  over style suggestions
- Propose concrete, ranked improvements to topics, ordering, scope, and audience
  fit

# Workflow

## Read the Material
- Read `.claude/templates/book_map.template.md` for the expected TOC structure

- Read `book_map.md`, which stores the `### Topics` of the book's TOC
  - Read `**Title**` and `**Target audience**` at the top of `book_map.md`
  - Read the `# Part` heading description the chapter belongs to
  - Read the target chapter's `### Topics` that the user refers to
  - Ignore all other sections
    - I.e., `### Lessons`, `### Tutorials`, `### Related packages`,
      `### Related books`, `### Related papers`
  - Read the `### Topics` of sibling chapters in that Part and the immediate
    neighbors, chapter N-1 and N+1, to judge continuity

## Criticize
- Read `.claude/skills/text.criticize/SKILL.md` for general review approaches

- Evaluate these axes, reporting only high-confidence issues:
  - **Internal flow**:
    - Order of the `### Topics` bullets
    - Prerequisite ordering
    - Redundant or overlapping bullets
    - A bullet that is really two topics
  - **Cross-chapter flow**:
    - Overlap with neighbors or others in the same Part
    - A topic that belongs earlier or later
    - Forward references to concepts not yet introduced
  - **Part fit**:
    - Does the chapter match the scope description of its `# Part` (foundations
      vs. advanced theory vs. deployment)
    - Flag misplaced chapters
  - **Structure conformance**:
    - Compare the structure to `.claude/templates/book_map.template.md`
    - Report:
      - Parts that don't follow the subsections
      - Lessons without a FULL/PART/WEAK tag
      - References not following `.claude/skills/references.rules.md`
  - **Audience fit**:
    - Matches the stated audience
    - Level too high or low
    - Assumed background
    - Unexplained jargon
  - **Scope and balance**:
    - Too much or too little content for one chapter
    - Candidates to split or merge

- Rank each issue by severity:
  - **CRITICAL**: breaks the chapter's logic or misplaces it
  - **HIGH**: misleads or confuses the reader
  - **MEDIUM**: hurts clarity or completeness
  - **LOW**: minor polish

## Write Result
- Write results using the same format and file as in
  `## Step 4: Write the Results` in `.claude/skills/text.criticize/SKILL.md`

## Wait for Approval
- Present the criticism to the user
- Wait for the user to select items by index and give corrections
- Only then edit `book_map.md`, updating every section it affects (Topics,
  Lessons, Tutorials, Related packages, Related books, Related papers)

# Verification
- [ ] Confirm each reported issue cites the exact `### Topics` bullet or
      chapter it refers to
- [ ] Confirm no edit to `book_map.md` was made before the user approved it
- [ ] Confirm applied corrections update every affected section (Topics,
      Lessons, Tutorials, Related packages, Related books, Related papers)

skills.name: book_chapter.fix_headings
skills.desc: Fix Typst book chapter headings and slide titles to match its .smd source
skills.body:
---
description: Fix Typst book chapter headings and slide titles to match its .smd source
model: sonnet
---

# Goal

- Given a lecture's `.smd` source and its generated `.typ` book chapter (from
  `gen_book_chapter.py --mode typst_aima`), fix the heading levels and slide-title
  handling to follow the "Structural Hierarchy" rule in
  `.claude/skills/typst.rules.md`
- Mostly mechanical (moving `=`/`==`/`===` markers). A slide title that must become
  a transition (see Step 3) needs one reworded sentence. That is the only text this
  skill may change. The rest of the prose stays untouched
- A fix-up for chapters generated before that rule existed, or hand-edited
  inconsistently. On a chapter that already follows the rule, it is a no-op

# Inputs

- `<SMD_FILE>`: the lecture source
  - E.g., `msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.1-A_Map_of_Machine_Learning.smd`
- `<TYP_FILE>`: the generated book chapter for `<SMD_FILE>`
  - E.g., `msml610/book/Lesson02.1-A_Map_of_Machine_Learning.typ`

# Workflow

## Classify Every Heading/slide in `<SMD_FILE>`

- Walk `<SMD_FILE>` top to bottom, collecting every `#`/`##`/`###`(+) heading line
  and every `* Slide Title` line, in source order, with its line number
- Track one running flag, `seen_subheading`, starting `False`: flip it to `True` the
  first time a `##` or deeper heading is seen. Its value when each `* Slide Title`
  line is reached (before any `##` on the same line updates it) is what Step 3
  needs for that slide

## Locate the Matching Line in `<TYP_FILE>`

- `<TYP_FILE>` carries a
  ```text
  // From: <SMD_FILE>:<LINE_NUMBER> '<MARKER> <TITLE>'
  // Slide: <TITLE>
  ```
  comment immediately above every heading/slide it was generated from.
  Match each Step 1 entry by line number + marker, not by title alone, since titles
  can repeat (e.g., a lesson and its own first slide sharing a name)
- The heading/title line itself is the next non-comment line after
  `// Slide: <TITLE>`: it may currently be `#strong[Title]`, `= Title` / `== Title`
  / `=== Title`, or missing entirely (the block's paragraph starts right after the
  comment, no title line at all)

## Apply the Rule From `typst.rules.md`

// TODO(ai_gp): Make reference to the typst.rules.md instead of this wall of text
For each block from Step 2, make its title line match the `## Structural Hierarchy`
and `## Mandatory Sections` rules in `typst.rules.md`. This skill decides *which*
rule applies to each block. The rules define the heading syntax:
- **H1** (`#`), title equal to the chapter title in `#chapter(...)` (the common
  case: one `#` per lesson): delete the title line, keep the `// From:`/`// Slide:`
  comments. If a body-level H1 has _different_ text, check for `##`/`###` under it
  before the next `#` (or end of document). With no nested subsections, use
  `#strong[Title]` instead of deleting it. With nested `##`/`###` subsections (e.g.,
  a lesson combining two topics, each `# Topic` with its own `##` subsections), keep
  a real `= Title` heading, since `typst.rules.md` forbids `#strong` in place of a
  heading. If unsure, cross-check `extract_toc_from_txt.py -i <SMD_FILE>` vs
  `grep "^=" <TYP_FILE>`
- **`##`/`###`/deeper**: apply the `## Structural Hierarchy` heading-level mapping.
  Leave alone if already correct
- **`* Roadmap`**, **`* Summary`**, **`* References`**: always the mandatory level-1
  headings per `## Mandatory Sections`, whatever `seen_subheading` is. The
  `seen_subheading` rule below covers ordinary slides only and never applies to them
- **`* Slide Title`** (any other slide):
  - `seen_subheading` was `False` -> `= Title`, a real heading (add the line if
    missing, replace `#strong[Title]` or a transitioned-in paragraph)
  - `seen_subheading` was `True`, and this is the first slide since that heading
    (no other `* Slide Title` block since) -> drop the title: no `#strong[Title]`
    line, no added transition. Delete a `#strong[Title]` line if present (and the
    blank line after it). The paragraph opens with its own first sentence, directly
    after the `// Slide:` comment
  - `seen_subheading` was `True`, and at least one other slide appeared since that
    heading -> drop the title and transition in from the previous slide's ending
    instead of restating the title:
    - Read the previous block's last sentence and this block's first sentence
    - If the previous sentence already works as a lead-in (a forward reference, a
      rhetorical question, a "this raises the question of X" close) and the
      paragraph's opening picks it up, deleting the title line is enough
    - Otherwise, prepend one short sentence (or reword the first clause of the
      opening sentence) that connects the two: a callback to the previous slide's
      last term or claim, a contrast ("beyond X, a second axis is..."), or an
      explicit bridge. Keep it to one sentence. Do not summarize or repeat what the
      paragraph says next
    - A slide's central term may get `#strong[...]` inside the transition or the
      first sentence, never on its own line
  - Either way, remove the blank line between the title line and the body: the
    comment block is followed directly by the paragraph (see the "Good" examples in
    `typst.rules.md`)
Never touch `#strong[...]`/`#emph[...]` elsewhere in the prose (mid-paragraph terms,
list lead phrases). Never touch sentences beyond the first of a transitioned-in
paragraph. Only the title lines from Step 2 and the opening sentence next to them
are in scope

# Verification

- [ ] Lint the file: `typstyle --inplace --wrap-text -l 85 <TYP_FILE>`
- [ ] Compile and check the PDF looks right: see
      `.claude/skills/book.fix_rendered_pdf/SKILL.md`
- [ ] Confirm no prose beyond the in-scope title lines and their opening
      sentence was changed

    line, no added transition. Delete a `#strong[Title]` line if present (and the
    blank line after it). The paragraph opens with its own first sentence, directly
    after the `// Slide:` comment
  - `seen_subheading` was `True`, and at least one other slide appeared since that
    heading -> drop the title and transition in from the previous slide's ending
    instead of restating the title:
    - Read the previous block's last sentence and this block's first sentence
    - If the previous sentence already works as a lead-in (a forward reference, a
      rhetorical question, a "this raises the question of X" close) and the
      paragraph's opening picks it up, deleting the title line is enough
    - Otherwise, prepend one short sentence (or reword the first clause of the
      opening sentence) that connects the two: a callback to the previous slide's
      last term or claim, a contrast ("beyond X, a second axis is..."), or an
      explicit bridge. Keep it to one sentence. Do not summarize or repeat what the
      paragraph says next
    - A slide's central term may get `#strong[...]` inside the transition or the
      first sentence, never on its own line
  - Either way, remove the blank line between the title line and the body: the
    comment block is followed directly by the paragraph (see the "Good" examples in
    `typst.rules.md`)
Never touch `#strong[...]`/`#emph[...]` elsewhere in the prose (mid-paragraph terms,
list lead phrases). Never touch sentences beyond the first of a transitioned-in
paragraph. Only the title lines from Step 2 and the opening sentence next to them
are in scope

# Verification

- [ ] Lint the file: `typstyle --inplace --wrap-text -l 85 <TYP_FILE>`
- [ ] Compile and check the PDF looks right: see
      `.claude/skills/book.fix_rendered_pdf/SKILL.md`
- [ ] Confirm no prose beyond the in-scope title lines and their opening
      sentence was changed

# Goal
- Review book chapters and add bold and italic where needed

# Workflow

## Gather Context
- Read `.claude/skills/book_map.rules.md`

## Identify Chapters to Process
- For multiple chapters, process each one independently, applying every step below

## Detect File Type
- Detect the type from its extension:
  - `.typ`: Typst
  - `.tex`: Latex
  - `.md`: markdown
- If the extension is missing or ambiguous, infer the type from existing
  markup (e.g., `#emph[...]` implies Typst)

## Render Bold and Italic Based on the Type of File
- Render bold:
  - `#strong[...]` in Typst
  - `\textbf{...}` in Latex
  - `**...**` in markdown
- Render italic:
  - `#emph[...]` in Typst
  - `\textit{...}` in Latex
  - `_..._` in markdown

## Detect Chapter Type
- A chapter is Roadmap or Summary type if its title or heading contains
  "Roadmap", "Summary", or "Overview"
- Every other chapter is a regular chapter

## Improve Roadmap and Summary Chapters
- Do not use bold
- Use italic for terms that are introduced and important

### Example: Summary Chapter

- **Bad** (no italic on introduced terms)
  ```text
  From there, the discussion turns to the languages available for encoding knowledge,
  spanning natural language, programming languages, propositional logic, and
  first-order logic, each offering a different point in that tradeoff space. Semantics
  then pins down what it means for a knowledge base to be "about" the world: how
  symbols are grounded in referents, what a model is, and what it means for a sentence
  to be satisfied. Reasoning builds on that semantic foundation by defining entailment
  (what follows from what), inference (the mechanical process of deriving new
  sentences), and the twin guarantees of soundness and completeness that connect the
  two. With these pieces in place, the focus shifts to agents that actually use
  represented knowledge: from simple reflex agents, through rule-based systems, to full
  knowledge-based agents that maintain an internal knowledge base and query it before
  acting. Finally, ontologies provide the large-scale organizational scaffolding,
  specifying the categories, relations, and axioms that let knowledge be shared and
  reused across tasks and domains.
  ```

- **Good** (italic marks each introduced term)
  ```text
  From there, the discussion turns to the #emph[languages] available for encoding
  knowledge, spanning natural language, programming languages, propositional logic, and
  first-order logic, each offering a different point in that tradeoff space.
  #emph[Semantics] then pins down what it means for a knowledge base to be "about" the
   world: how symbols are grounded in referents, what a model is, and what it means for
   a sentence to be satisfied. #emph[Reasoning] builds on that semantic foundation by
   defining #emph[entailment] (what follows from what), #emph[inference] (the
   mechanical process of deriving new sentences), and the twin guarantees of
   #emph[soundness] and #emph[completeness] that connect the two. With these pieces in
   place, the focus shifts to #emph[agents] that actually use represented knowledge:
   from simple reflex agents, through rule-based systems, to full knowledge-based
   agents that maintain an internal knowledge base and query it before acting. Finally,
   #emph[ontologies] provide the large-scale organizational scaffolding, specifying the
  categories, relations, and axioms that let knowledge be shared and reused across
  tasks and domains.
  ```

## Improve Other Chapters
- Use bold for definitions of a term
- Use italic to highlight important concepts

### Example: Apply Bold to Chapter

- **Bad** (no bold on the defined terms)
  ```text
  KR defines two essential aspects of any encoding. Syntax determines
  how knowledge is organized: whether as a flat set of propositions, a hierarchy
  of classes and instances, or a graph of interconnected concepts.
  Semantics determines what the encoded statements actually mean: the
  formal interpretation that lets a reasoner distinguish valid inferences from
  invalid ones. Without clear semantics, a knowledge base is just syntax; without
  clear structure, it becomes unwieldy as the domain grows.
  ```

- **Good** (bold marks each defined term)
  ```text
  KR defines two essential aspects of any encoding. #strong[Syntax] determines
  how knowledge is organized: whether as a flat set of propositions, a hierarchy
  of classes and instances, or a graph of interconnected concepts.
  #strong[Semantics] determines what the encoded statements actually mean: the
  formal interpretation that lets a reasoner distinguish valid inferences from
  invalid ones. Without clear semantics, a knowledge base is just syntax; without
  clear structure, it becomes unwieldy as the domain grows.
  ```

### Example: Apply Italic to Chapter

- **Bad** (no italic on the highlighted concepts)
  ```text
  Machines need to reason about the world, not just recognize patterns. A
  medical AI trained on patient data can predict diseases with impressive
  accuracy, but to explain a diagnosis to a doctor, it needs structured
  knowledge that captures relationships between symptoms, conditions, and
  treatments. Without that structure, prediction divorced from reasoning is
  often useless.
  ```

- **Good** (italic marks each highlighted concept)
  ```text
  Machines need to #emph[reason] about the world, not just recognize patterns. A
  medical AI trained on patient data can #emph[predict] diseases with impressive
  accuracy, but to #emph[explain] a diagnosis to a doctor, it needs structured
  knowledge that captures relationships between symptoms, conditions, and
  treatments. Without that structure, prediction divorced from reasoning is
  often useless.
  ```

## Write Result
- Update the file with the improved text

# Constraints
- Do not tag a term that is already bold or italic
- Do not change wording: only add tags around existing text
- Limit density to 1-2 tagged terms per paragraph so tags keep their signal
- Leave fenced code blocks, math, and citations untouched

# Verification
- [ ] Diff the file before and after: confirm only tags were added, with no
      wording changed, removed, or reordered
- [ ] Confirm tag density is reasonable: not every sentence has a tagged term
- [ ] For Typst or Latex files, render the chapter to confirm the tags compile
      without errors

description: Update a book's content to match changes in its source file
model: opus
---

# Goal
- Given a book content file `<TARGET>` (markdown or tex) and its source file
  `<SOURCE>`, find the changes in `<SOURCE>` and incorporate them into `<TARGET>`

# Workflow

## Read the Version Header
- `<SOURCE>` has a header with the Git hash and timestamp of the material used to
  generate the current `<TARGET>`
  - E.g.,
    ```text
    % git_hash=<GIT_HASH>, timestamp=<TIMESTAMP>
    % <SOURCE>
    ```
  - E.g.,
    ```text
    % git_hash=f15bc6b9, timestamp=2026-07-15 14:41:12 EDT
    % book_springer/lectures_source/Lesson02.1_From_Data_Science_To_Decision_Science.txt
    ```
- Get the diff of `<SOURCE>` since `<GIT_HASH>` once, up front, not per section:
  ```bash
  > git diff <GIT_HASH> -- <SOURCE>
  ```

## Incorporate Changes
- Modify `<TARGET>` to reflect every change in `<SOURCE>` since `<GIT_HASH>`
- Follow the style of `<TARGET>`, reading the matching `.claude/skills/*.rules.md`
- `<TARGET>` may be a superset of `<SOURCE>`. A `.typ` chapter routinely adds
  headings, diagrams, or paragraphs that group or expand several flat `.smd` slides
  (see "Structural Hierarchy" in `typst.rules.md`)
  - If `<SOURCE>` drops a heading or diagram that `<TARGET>` built on, keep the
    `<TARGET>` content, since it has no direct counterpart anymore
  - Remove it only if the diff shows the underlying fact or example was changed or
    retracted, not merely reorganized out of the slide deck
- Update the header at the top of `<TARGET>` to the new hash and timestamp:
  ```text
  // git_hash=<NEW_GIT_HASH> timestamp=<NEW_TIMESTAMP>
  ```

## Compare Entire Flow
- Make the flow of `<TARGET>` (typst, latex, or md) follow the flow of `<SOURCE>`
- E.g., run `extract_toc_from_txt.py` on both files and compare
  ```bash
  > extract_toc_from_txt.py -i msml610/lectures_source/Lesson03.3-Non_classical_logics.smd

  > extract_toc_from_txt.py -i msml610/book/Lesson03.3-Non_classical_logics.typ
  ```
- Ensure the flow of `<TARGET>` is consistent with `<SOURCE>`

## Update Source-Line References
- A `.typ` `<TARGET>` has a `// From: <SOURCE>:<LINE> '<slide title>'` comment above
  each section, pointing to the exact `<SOURCE>` line it was generated from
- An edit above a slide shifts every later line number. After incorporating the
  changes, walk the `// From:` comments top to bottom and fix each `<LINE>` so it
  matches the slide's current position in `<SOURCE>`
  - Find a slide by grepping `<SOURCE>` for its `*` or `#` title

## Update Rendered Images
- If the diff changes a `graphviz`/`mermaid`/`tikz`/... code block (new styling, new
  nodes, or a static image swapped for a rendered diagram, or vice versa), carry the
  same change into the matching `rendered_images:begin`/`rendered_images:end`
  placeholder in `<TARGET>` (see "Diagram Placeholders and `wrap-content`" in
  `typst.rules.md`)
- Never edit the numbered `.png` files (`<Chapter>.typ.figs/<Chapter>.<N>.png`)
  or the `#figure(image(...))` calls by hand for content that already renders
  correctly. `render_images.py` regenerates both on the next render
- If a section gains or loses a rendered figure, every later `<N>` shifts. After
  editing the placeholders, grep `<TARGET>` for `\.typ\.figs/.*\.[0-9]+\.png` and
  renumber every `#figure(image(...))` call, and its matching `label=`/`caption=`
  line, sequentially from 1 in document order
- Carry caption or label wording changes like prose. If the diff renames or rewords
  what a diagram depicts, update the figure's `caption=`/`caption:` per "Figures:
  Required Elements" in `typst.rules.md` (sentence case, one plain line, no
  node-by-node listing)

# Verification
- [ ] Confirm every change in `<SOURCE>` since `<GIT_HASH>` is reflected in
      `<TARGET>`
- [ ] Confirm `<TARGET>` still follows the style of its `.claude/skills/*.rules.md`
      (`typst.rules.md`, `latex.rules.md`, or `markdown.rules.md`)
- [ ] Confirm `<TARGET>` compiles
  - For `.typ`, use `render_book_chapter.py -i <TARGET>` if Docker and graphviz work
  - Lighter syntax-only check without Docker. It avoids the image-tagging bug of
    `render_book_chapter.py` and re-rendering of sibling `.typ` files under a
    running `gen_slides.py --daemon`: stub the unrendered figure PNGs, then compile
    ```bash
    > typst compile --root . <TARGET> /tmp/check.pdf
    ```
  - After either check, `git status`/`git diff` the whole book directory, not just
    `<TARGET>`, to catch side effects on sibling chapters
- [ ] Confirm every `// From: <SOURCE>:<LINE>` comment points to the current line
      in `<SOURCE>`
- [ ] Confirm every figure's numbered `.png` filename is sequential in document
      order, with no gaps or duplicates

skills.desc: Renumber a book map, reorder its Detailed TOC to follow the Short TOC, and rename the matching lecture and tutorial files
skills.body:
---
description: Renumber a book map, reorder its Detailed TOC to follow the Short TOC, and rename the matching lecture and tutorial files
model: opus
---

# Goal

- Given a book map `<BOOK_MAP>` (e.g., `book_Modern_AI_for_Finance/book_map.md`),
  make it follow `.claude/skills/book_map.rules.md`:
  - Renumber the chapters
  - Reorder `# Detailed TOC` to follow `## Short TOC`
  - Keep the Roadmap table in sync
  - Rename the numbered files in `<BOOK>/lectures_source/` and
    `<BOOK>/tutorials/`, and fix the references to them
- Write a plan, wait for the user to approve it, then apply it

# Inputs

- `<BOOK_MAP>`: the book map to update
- `<BOOK>`: the directory that contains `<BOOK_MAP>`

# Workflow

## Read

- Read `.claude/skills/book_map.rules.md` and `<BOOK_MAP>` in full
- Use `.claude/templates/book_map.template.md` for the structure of new chapters
- Follow `.claude/skills/markdown.rules.md` and `.claude/skills/text.rules.md`
  for any text you add

## Compute the New Numbers

- `## Short TOC` is the source of truth for chapter order, parts, and part names
  - Do not trust the chapter numbers in the file
- Match chapters across Short TOC, Detailed TOC, and Roadmap by title
  - Treat titles that differ only in case, `and`, or a trailing `s` as equal
- Number the chapters `01`, `02`, ... in Short TOC order, with no gaps
  - Number the entries marked `?` too
- Keep the map `old number -> new number`

## Map the Files

- Look recursively in `<BOOK>/lectures_source/` and `<BOOK>/tutorials/`
- A name is numbered when `Lesson` or `L` is followed by `<NN>` and `.` or `_`
  - E.g., `Lesson05.01_Forecasting.smd`, `L05_forecasting/`,
    `L05_01_forecasting.ipynb`, `figures/L05.01.Drawdown.png`
- Skip `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `*.log`, `OLD/`, `old/`, and names with no number
- Assign each file to a chapter:
  - First by the file name in the Roadmap, `### Slides`, or `### Tutorials`
  - Then by the old number in the name
- Build the new name by replacing only `<NN>`
  - Keep `<MM>`, the title, and the extension
- Do not rename a file when the two rules disagree or no chapter matches: ask
  under `## Questions`

## Write the Plan

- Create `plan-book_map.update.md` next to `<BOOK_MAP>`
- Write a checkbox list with a global index per item, so the user can approve by
  index
- Make each item state the exact change, the line number, and the reason
- Group the items under these headers, omitting the empty ones:
  - `## Short TOC`, `## Parts`, `## Renumbering`, `## Reordering`,
    `## New Chapters`, `## Chapters Without a Short TOC Entry`, `## Roadmap`,
    `## Cross References`, `## Lecture Files`, `## Tutorials`,
    `## File References`, `## Findings Not Fixed`, `## Questions`

Propose these changes:
- **Short TOC**: nested bullets (part, then `<NN>, <Title>`, then topics)
- **Parts**: make `# Part` headings and Roadmap part rows use the Short TOC names
  and order, keeping the numeral style of the file
- **Titles**: use the Short TOC title in the three places
  - Ask when the meaning differs, not only the wording
- **Renumbering and reordering**: one item per chapter that changes
  - Move a chapter as one block, from its `## <NN>:` heading to the next `##`
- **New chapter** (in Short TOC, not in Detailed TOC): create the section from
  the Chapter Template
  - Fill `### Goals` with 3 bullets and `### Topics` from the Short TOC
  - Write `### Slides` as `- N/A: no dedicated deck yet`
  - Write `### Lesson Materials` with only `_Not covered_` and a
    `// TODO(gp): Fill the lesson materials` line
  - Do not invent coverage percentages
- **Chapter without a Short TOC entry**: never propose to delete it
  - Ask: add it to the Short TOC, merge it into a chapter, or remove it
- **Roadmap**: reorder and renumber the rows, keep the cell values, and use the
  new file names in the cells
- **Cross references**: replace old chapter numbers in prose (`chapter 02`)
- **Lecture files and tutorials**: one item per chapter and directory, listing
  each `old path -> new path`
  - Keep a tutorial directory and its files in one item, since the notebook,
    its `.py`, and `_utils.py` import each other by name
- **File references**: one item per file that uses an old name, as
  `<path>:<line>: <old> -> <new>`
  - Look in `<BOOK_MAP>`, the renamed files (figure paths, `import` lines), and
    other book maps or `// From:` comments in this repo
  - For other Git repos, point to `.claude/skills/git.update_references/SKILL.md`
- **`// TODO(ai_gp):` markers**: remove a marker the plan resolves, and list the
  others under `## Questions`

Report only these, since they need content judgment:
- Missing chapter subsection
- `### Goals` without 3 bullets, or a bullet of 100 characters or more
- `### Topics` over 25 lines or 200 words
- `### Lesson Materials` pointing to `<BOOK>/lectures_source/*.smd`
- Short TOC topics that differ from `### Topics`
- Wrong coverage percentages
- For a content review, point to `.claude/skills/book.criticize_toc/SKILL.md`

## Wait for Approval

- Print only the plan path and the item count
- Wait for the user to approve items by index, or to give corrections

## Apply the Approved Items

- Edit `<BOOK_MAP>` in this order, so the line numbers in the plan stay valid:
  - Cross references, Roadmap, Detailed TOC (move, renumber, add), Short TOC
- Rename files with `git mv` (see `.claude/skills/git.move/SKILL.md`), in two
  phases, because renumbering permutes the numbers (`02 -> 03`, `03 -> 04`):
  - Move every approved path to `tmp.<new name>`
  - Move every `tmp.<new name>` to its final path
  - Rename a directory before the files in it
- Update the references with one mapping `old name -> new name`, applied in a
  single pass per file, so that a replacement is never replaced again
  - Replace whole names only, never a bare `L02` or `Lesson02`
- Format `<BOOK_MAP>`:
  ```bash
  > lint_text.py -i <BOOK_MAP>
  ```
- Show a summary: renumbered, moved, and renamed items, and anything left open

# Constraints

- Do not edit anything before the user approves the plan
- Do not change a chapter's text, except its `## <NN>:` heading, its chapter
  number cross references, and the edits in an approved item
- Do not delete a chapter, a topic, a Lesson Materials bullet, or a file
- Do not rename a file outside `<BOOK>/lectures_source/` and `<BOOK>/tutorials/`
- Do not change the content of a lecture or tutorial file, except the references
  to renamed files
- Do not guess coverage percentages
- Do not commit: leave the changes in the working tree

# Example

```markdown
## Renumbering
- [ ] 1. `## 05: Price and Volatility Forecasting` -> `## 07: Forecasting`
      (line 561): Short TOC position 7

## Reordering
- [ ] 2. Move `## 07` (lines 561-690) after `## 06` (line 1012)

## Lecture Files
- [ ] 3. Chapter `05 -> 07`, `lectures_source/`
  - `Lesson05.01_Forecasting.smd` -> `Lesson07.01_Forecasting.smd`
  - `figures/L05.01.Drawdown.png` -> `figures/L07.01.Drawdown.png`

## Tutorials
- [ ] 4. Chapter `05 -> 07`, `tutorials/`
  - `L05_forecasting/` -> `L07_forecasting/`
  - `L05_forecasting/L05_01_forecasting.ipynb` ->
    `L07_forecasting/L07_01_forecasting.ipynb`

## File References
- [ ] 5. `book_map.md:145`: `Lesson05.01_Forecasting.smd` ->
      `Lesson07.01_Forecasting.smd`
```

# Verification

- [ ] Confirm chapter numbers are consecutive, zero-padded, with no `?` left
- [ ] Confirm `## <NN>:` headings, Roadmap rows, and part names follow the Short
      TOC order
- [ ] Confirm no prose reference uses an old chapter number
- [ ] Confirm every numbered file under `lectures_source/` and `tutorials/` has
      the number of its chapter
- [ ] Confirm `git status --short <BOOK>` shows renames, and no `tmp.*` is left
- [ ] Confirm `grep -rF "<old name>" .` finds nothing
- [ ] Confirm `python -I -m py_compile` passes on the renamed tutorial `.py`
      files
- [ ] Confirm `lint_text.py -i <BOOK_MAP>` completes without errors

skills.name: bookmark.add
skills.desc: Find the research idea or blog file related to given links and add a TODO
skills.body:
---
description: Find the research idea or blog file related to given links and add a TODO
model: haiku
---

# Goal
- Given one or more links `<LINKS>`, find the file(s) among the following that are
  related to each link, and add a TODO to the most related file:
  - `research/ideas/*.md`
  - `website/docs/blog/posts/*.md`
  ```text
  // TODO(gp): incorporate the link <LINK> to <TOPIC>
  ```

# Workflow

## Collect Material
- Read the title and content of each link in `<LINKS>` (use `WebFetch` if the URL
  alone is not descriptive enough to judge the topic)
- List all candidate files in the two dirs above

## Match Links to Files
- For each link, compare its topic with each candidate's title, headers, and first
  paragraph. Rank candidates by relevance
- Pick the single best match for each link
  - If several files are close, list them and ask the user which to use
  - If no file plausibly matches, do not force a match. Report it instead

## Add the TODO
- In the matched file, add one line:
  ```text
  // TODO(gp): incorporate the link <LINK> to <TOPIC>
  ```
  where `<TOPIC>` is a short description (under 15 words) of the relevant part of
  the link, e.g., a technique, a result, or a quote
- Placement:
  - If the file has a top-of-file `// TODO(gp): ...` block, add the new line as an
    adjacent line in that block
  - Otherwise, put it near the most related section, e.g., right above the relevant
    bullet point or paragraph
- Change no other content in the file
- If several links map to one file, add one TODO line per link

## Report
- For each link, print the file it was added to and the exact TODO line inserted
- Report any unmatched link explicitly. Do not skip it silently

# Verification
- [ ] Each link matches at most one file, with no forced or guessed match
- [ ] Each inserted line follows the exact `// TODO(gp): incorporate the link <LINK>
  to <TOPIC>` format
- [ ] No content other than the new TODO line(s) changed in the matched file
- [ ] The report lists every link with its target file or "not matched" status

---
description: Annotate file with TODOs based on the convention and rule violations
model: haiku
---

# Goal
- Annotate the file `<FILE>` with TODOs for each violated rule and convention

# Workflow

## Determine the Rules to Apply
- If `<FILE>` is a Python file, use `<RULES>`
  - `.claude/skills/coding.rules.md`
- If `<FILE>` is a Python testing file (e.g., `test/test_*.py`), use `<RULES>`
  - `.claude/skills/coding.rules.md`
  - `.claude/skills/testing.rules.md`
- Print the rule files `<RULES>` used for each file in `<FILE>`
- Read the rule files `<RULES>` carefully

## Annotate with TODOs
- Annotate every point in `<FILE>` that violates `<RULES>`, adding a TODO
  before it, like
  ```python
  # TODO(ai_gp): Apply <RULE> before the point with violation
  ```

skills.desc: Identify private or public functions in a file and rename with underscore
skills.body:
---
description: Identify private or public functions in a file and rename with underscore
model: haiku
---

# Goal
For each function `<FUNC>` in the passed Python file `<FILE>`, decide if it is
private or public by checking whether Python files or Jupyter notebooks outside
`<FILE>` call it.

# Conventions
- Follow `## Mark Private Functions` in `.claude/skills/coding.rules.md`

# Definitions

## External Files
- **External files** = any Python file or Jupyter notebook outside the target
  file
  - Including:
    - Sibling scripts in the same package (e.g., `notes_to_pdf.py` calling
      functions from `lib_notes_to_pdf.py`)
    - Parent/sibling modules that import from the target
    - CLI entry point scripts
  - Excluding:
    - Test files of the target. A function stays private even if a test calls it

- **Note:** Functions in a library module's public API are PUBLIC, even if no
  `__main__` entry point calls them. Utilities that other scripts in the package
  import are PUBLIC too

# Private Functions
- If `<FUNC>` is not called by any external file, it is private: rename it with a
  `_` prefix
  - E.g., `def function` -> `def _function`
  - Include only internal utilities, helpers, and implementation details
- Update all callers of `<FUNC>` to the new name

- **Good** (only called within its own file, so renamed private)
  ```python
  # lib_helper.py
  def public_function():
      _internal_helper()  # Only called within this file, so private.

  def _internal_helper():
      pass
  ```

# Public Functions
- If `<FUNC>` is called by external files, it is public: its name must not start
  with `_`
  - This includes functions in shared utility modules that sibling scripts call
- Update all callers, external and internal, to the new name

- **Good** (called by an external file, so it stays public)
  ```python
  # lib_notes_to_pdf.py
  def preprocess_notes(file_name, prefix):  # Called by notes_to_pdf.py, so public.
      _internal_step_1(file_name)  # Private helper.

  def _internal_step_1(file_name):  # Only used within lib_notes_to_pdf.py, so private.
      pass
  ```

# Workflow

## Find All Functions
- Find all functions in `<FILE>`

## Search for External Calls
- For each function, search the whole codebase:
  ```bash
  grep -r "<FUNC>" --include="*.py" --include="*.ipynb" --exclude="test_*.py"
  ```

## Classify and Rename
- Classify each function as public or private from its external usage
- Rename functions and update all call sites (in both files)
- Verify the changes

# Verification
- [ ] Grep the entire codebase to confirm all calls were renamed correctly
      ```bash
      grep -r "old_name\|new_name" --include="*.py" --include="*.ipynb"
      ```
- [ ] Run pyright to verify type correctness of modified function invocations
- [ ] Run unit tests for the modified files to ensure nothing broke
